label: Illustrative toy inputs chosen so every step can be checked by hand with a calculator. They are not real model weights, activations or logits.

rmsnorm.equation: y_i = x_i / sqrt( (1/d) * sum_j x_j^2 + eps ) * gamma_i

eps_effect.note: eps = 1e-05 is negligible here: it changes the RMS from 2.500000 to 2.500002. It only matters when every x_i is close to 0, where it prevents a division by zero.

x_over_rms_mean_squares.note: after dividing by the RMS the mean of squares is 1 (minus the eps effect)

gamma.note: toy values; in a real model gamma is a learned vector of length d_model

rmsnorm.no_mean_subtraction: RMSNorm only rescales; unlike LayerNorm it does not subtract the mean and has no bias.
rmsnorm.why_pre_norm: Each layer computes H = X + Attention(RMSNorm(X)) and X' = H + MLP(RMSNorm(H)): the norm sits inside the residual branch, so the residual stream itself is never normalised. With this pre-norm layout the gradients near the output are well-behaved at initialisation and training needs no learning-rate warm-up stage; post-norm needs it.

real_model.note: M-dense does the same arithmetic over 12,288 values per token, before attention and before the MLP in every layer.

sources.formula: research/notes/05-papers-architecture.md §2.A A2 [S2 Zhang & Sennrich 2019, eq. 4]; eps is an implementation detail added inside the square root (class B)

attention.equation: O = softmax( Q K^T / sqrt(d_head) + M ) V
attention.inputs_note: Row i of Q, K, V belongs to token i. In a model they come from X·W_q, X·W_k, X·W_v.

step1_dot_products.note: Entry (i, j) is q_i · k_j: how strongly token i's query matches token j's key. All 16 are computed, including the future ones the mask removes next.

step2_scale.why: Dividing by sqrt(d_head) keeps the dot products' spread roughly independent of d_head, so softmax does not saturate when d_head is large (128 in M-dense).

step3_mask.rule: M[i][j] = 0 if j <= i, -inf if j > i (above the diagonal)
step3_mask.why_no_future: Token i is generated before tokens i+1, i+2, ... exist, so during generation there is nothing to look at. Training and prefill process all positions at once, so the future keys ARE in memory; the mask adds -inf to every score with j > i. exp(-inf) = 0, so those keys get weight exactly 0 and contribute nothing to token i's output. This keeps prefill (all tokens at once) and decode (one token at a time) consistent: token i's result is mathematically the same either way.

online_softmax.algorithm: FlashAttention-2 style recurrence for one query row: keep a running max m, a running sum l of exp(score - m) and an unnormalised accumulator acc. For each tile of keys: m_new = max(m, max(tile scores)); rescale = exp(m - m_new); p = exp(tile scores - m_new); l = rescale*l + sum(p); acc = rescale*acc + p·V_tile. At the end, output = acc / l.
online_softmax.why_rescale: Earlier tiles were exponentiated relative to an older, smaller max. Multiplying by exp(m_old - m_new) converts them to the new max, so the result equals one softmax over all keys. The full score row never has to exist at once.

rescale_old.text: exp(m_old - m_new) = exp(-inf) = 0 (first tile: nothing to rescale)

p.text: exp(score - m_new) for each key in the tile

steps.reason: every key in this tile is after token 0 (j > 0), so the whole tile is masked; causal FlashAttention kernels skip such tiles

output.text: acc / l (one division at the end)

online_softmax.identity: Online softmax gives exactly the same output as standard softmax (up to floating-point rounding; here the difference is below 1e-12). FlashAttention changes where the numbers live (tiles in on-chip SRAM instead of an L x L matrix in HBM), not the attention arithmetic.
